speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. J. A. CALDER (Minister of Immigration and 'Colonization) moved the second reading of Bill No. 120, to provide for the retirement of certain members of the public service.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this Bill is, I think, explained by the Bill itself. It is an Act to provide for the retirement of certain members of the public service. It will be remembered by the House that a somewhat similar measure was brought down by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) last year and, if I am not mistaken, it proceeded to the second reading and then was not advanced any farther, the reason being that upon consideration the Government finally decided that the provisions contained in the Bill of last session scarcely met the situation. Since then the problems involved have been re-considered with the result that the present measure is now before the House.
I am sure I need not refer at length to the conditions existing in the Civil Service. The matter has been one of discussion in this House ever since I have been here, and I presume for many years previously. There is not a member of the House who is not aware that there are defects in the Civil Service that should be remedied. I refer particularly to the over-manning, and also to the fact that there are a certain number in

the 'Civil Service of advanced age for whom no provision has been made for retirement simply because they do not comae under the existing Superannuation Acts. For these reasons the Government has thought it advisable to make some provisions whereby this problem may be dealt with, and that is the main object of this Bill. I do not know, Mr. Speaker, whether any particular party, or any particular Government, is chiefly responsible for the existing condition in the Civil Service. We simply know the condition exists, and my own idea is that all parties and all Governments-one might say ever since Confederation-are responsible for the system and the conditions that have grown up under it.
Now the problem of taking care of that situation and reasonably dealing with it, H must frankly say, in my judgment is a very difficult one, and I think it is because of this difficulty that all Governments in the past have hesitated to deal with it. One of the main difficulties is simply this: That the idea has prevailed to a very large extent that once a man gets into the service he is there for life. The idea prevails in Government circles, and in the 'Civil Service itself, that once appointed always appointed regardless of conditions that may grow up and regardless of whether or not the services of such men should be retained. Another phase of the difficulty has been this: That men have come into the service properly appointed, and have been in the service for long years. The time has arrived when they should be retired and there is no existing provision for their retirement in the way of any compensation, or allowance, or gratuity or annuity of any kind. For that reason all Governments have hesitated to retire these men from the service the result being that they remained there, regardless of their usefulness, practically until their decease. Well, we have come to the conclusion if Parliament will agree, that an attempt should be made to provide some measure whereby this condition can be remedied, and this Bill is submitted to the House for that purpose. The Government is not wedded to the details of the measure. We are anxious that there should be a full and free discussion of the details, and if suggestions can be made that will enable us to provide better means than is contained in this Bill for the purpose of taking hold of this problem I can assure the House the Government will welcome them. I would like to state briefly-because the Bill is not a very long one-what the chief
provisions are, in order that the House may grasp those clearly before we reach the committee stage.
In the first place the Bill provides that the Government may retire from the public service, either inside or outside, any employee whose services are not required, provision being made, however, in all cases for some allowance. The allowance in same cases may be very small, merely a gratuity; in other cases it may be an annuity as I shall explain later on. Let me state again, the Bill proposes to give the Government power to retire any officer in the Civil Service.

In the second case this provision is made: In the case of officers over 65 years of age the Civil Service .Commission, after consultation with the deputy heads of the departments, are required to report to the Government those who are not rendering good and efficient services, and all such officers so reported shall be retired. In the case of all officers under 65 years of age the Civil Service Commission-when requested by the Governor in Council and after consultation with the deputies-shall prepare lists of all officers and employees in the entire service who should be retired owing to advancing age, ill health, lack of experience or other cause, and the Governor in Council may order their retire-

speechtext: Yes. In the case of persons retired between the ages of 50 and 55 years, with at least 6 years' service, the allowance wo|uld be one month's salary for each two years' service. As an illustration, take the case of a man 52 years of age, who has given, we will say. 24 years' service: He would get one month's salary for each 2 years, in other words he would be'entitled to 12 months' salary. speechtext:
In the case ot persons retired between the ages of 55 and 60, yrith at least 5 years' service, the provision is that the lump sum allowance shall be 1 month's salary for each year of service with a maximum not exceeding 8 .months. In other wp/rds, if a man betwen those ages served fourteen years he would be entitled to one month's salary for each year of service, or 14 months' salary, except for the proviso that he is not to receive more than 8 months' salary. In the case of persons retired over the age of 60 years who lhave served at least 5 years hut- less than 10 years, the provision is the same as the last -those persons will be entitled to one month's salary for each year of service. All payments that I have referred to so far are lump sum payments.
As for persons retired over the age of 60 years, and who have seen at least ten years' service, the provision is tlhjat they shall be entitled for each year of service to one-sixtieth of the average salary they have received for the last 3 years. Under the old Superannuation Act the allowance was one-fiftieth with a maximum of thirty-five fiftieths if they served over 35 years. In this case pcrsotns over 60 years of age who have served more than 10 years will get an allowance of one-sixtieth with a maximum of thirty-sixtieths, or one-half of their salary and that is payable during their life.
This brief statement covers the provisions contained in this Bill. These allowances may be roughly divided into two classes. In the case of officers retired under the age of 60 years who have not seen 10 years' service provision is made for a lump sum gratuity running from 2 months up to 10 months' salary. In the case of officers over 60 years of age who have served for at least 10 years, provision is made for an annuity, the smallest amount payable being ten-sixtieths, or one-sixth of the average salary for the last 3 years, and the maximum amount allowed being thirty-sixtieths or one-half the salary paid for the last 3 years.

In reference to the point raised by the hon. member for Guysborough, the proviso to which he has referred applies only to those officials under 60 years of age who would be entitled under the Bill to a lump sum gratuity. If upon the joint certificate of the Civil Service Commission and the deputy head of a department it is reported that an officer who is retired by reason of physical disability or protracted illness should receive more than the lump sum gratuity provided by the Bill then the Government may pay an additional amount, not exceeding twice the sum provided for. But that is applicable only to persons retired who are entitled to a lump sum gratuity, not to those who are retired and are entitled to an annuity.
These are, briefly, the main provisions of the Bill. I am aware that there will be differences of opinon as to the provision that will be made to meet this situation; that members on both sides will have divergent views on the subject. However, I hope that as a result of our discussions some means will be arrived at of enabling the Government to deal with the problem. I am sure hon. members will agree that the condition in the service to which I have referred should not be allowed to continue. If it is thought that the provisions here made are not ample or are over-ample, any suggestions made in that regard will be welcomed by the Government. Last year the member

for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) expressed regret that the old superannuation law had been abolished; he thought that the situation to-day would be easier for everybody if that law had been continued in force. Personally, at the next session of Parliament I should like to see a proper Superannuation Bill brought down and enacted into law in order that the situation that has arisen as a result of what has taken place during the last fifteen, twenty, or thirty years may be dealt with. But the condition is bound to continue and to become intensified unless a proper superannuation law is provided. I move, Mr. Speaker, the second reading of the Bill.

Mr. Speaker, before the Bill is read the second time I should like to say a word or two. T have not taken occasion to study the Bill closely, because II did not think it would be pressed now that the session is drawing to an end. The'Bill is a very important one, affecting the future of a good many men and women who have devoted their lives to the service of the country. As I understand it, under the provisions of this Bill, after a civil servant has put in so many years' service, he is paid a lump sum based on his salary during a number of months and the length of time he has served, and then he is out. Mr. Speaker, it is with civil servants as with railwaymen; after they have served for twenty, twenty-five or thirty years in some line of Government work; after they have continued this length of time in one groove or followed a routine line of work, they are not in a position to take up any other line of business and fight their -way through. They are used to this work and they cannot familiarize themselves with or break themselves into new work. Under the provisions of this Bill men and women will be thrown on the street without any means of starting anew in order to earn a living. Under the circumstances this Bill ought to be referred to a committee or to some commission, with instructions to investigate the conditions and report upon what course should be adopted to protect these people. I admit, with the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Calder) that there are men in the service who are unable to perform their duties or to give to the country the service expected from them o.t the service that they ought to give. I admit that these persons should not be there; but sometimes it is not the fault of the civil servant that that is the case. I know from experience that as a per-

When my hon. friend (Mr. Burnham) rose to express his indignation that I should impute to civil servants the motive of trying to serve their country, I was going to point out that it is humiliating the men who have worked as civil servants all their lives-(I shall not hurt the feelings of my hon. friend (Mr. Burnham) by saying that they have served their country)-and who have spent all their earnings in the education of their children and the bringing up of their families, should upon retirement not be given enough to keep them in daily bread for the remainder of their days. I say it is humiliating; it is a condition that ought not to exist. We are very optimistic in everything that concerns our country. We are willing to take care of the people who inhabit our country. We have great resources; we are not afraid of the future. Are we to invite people to enter the Civil Service and tell them that when they reach a certain age and are not able any longer to render efficient service-because it is true that you cannot get the same service out of a man
who is well advanced in age that you were able to get in his earlier years,-upon the report of the proper officer they are to be dismissed with absolutely nothing to protect them in life.

The only way this question can be dealt with is for the Government of this country to establish a pension scheme for the whole Civil Service. If we want to raise the standard of efficiency of the Civil Service of this country, the Government should hold out to them some inducement in connection with the performance of their duty that they will be taken care of in their old age. The tendency of modern business is to make some provision for its employees of all classes', whether they toe engaged in menial work or something higher, that they may have some hope of reward when they

But the provision should be made by himself out of his own wages or salary, during his twenty-five, thirty, or forty years of service, just as you or I have to do. Civil servants, for instance, have twelve statutory holidays in the year. They have twenty-one .more days for 'their annual outing,-three .weeks. There is nothing in this country that we Jack so. much to-day as seM-reliance. Among the many repulsive words in the English language these two "tip" and "pension" I dislike the most. Why? speakeroldname: Mr. J. H. SINCLAIR (Antigonish and Guysborough):

speechtext:
Mi. Speaker I sympathize very strongly with the views expressed by the hon. member for West Elgin in reference to this matter. I do not see that there is any good reason why we should retire and provide for incapable men who have been but a short time in the public service. It is unreasonable that we should be asked to do that. We must be continuing to appoint incapable men. The Bill infers that we have such men in the public service. We know that during the last year or two complaints have been made by those at the head of departments that the men who are sent to them by the Civil Service Commission are incapable. We had the case of Commander Ross who could not carry on his work in the Pensions Department with the. staff that he had sent to him and he resigned. He himself was a good man, willing to do his best for the public but he found it necessary to give up his position altogether and resign from the public service because the men who were sent to him by the Civil Service Commission were incapable of doing the work. That appears to be the position. We are appointing people to the public service so fast that they have become so numerous that the matter looks hopeless to me. According to a statement made in the House this ses-

sion, we have appointed 25,000 men since the Armistice but that figure was revised by the hon. the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) and he said that only 12,000 of the 25,000 were still on the pay roll of the Government. That is about 660 every month since the Armistice and it is going at a pretty good rate. If a large proportion of those people that we are appointing are incapable of doing the work, and we make provision for retiring them without their contributing anything to the retirement fund, I must be allowed to place myself , on record against the principle of this Bill. I do not think it is necessary to make any long speech about it but I want it to be understood that I do not think the principle of the Bill is sound. I think we should wait until a Bill can be brought in that can provide for these people making some contribution out of their salaries for retirement. That is the only sound principle. If we are going to deal with this question at all, let us deal with it on business principles. There is no commercial company in the country-I suppose there is none in the world-that would do what we are doing today. If the bank employs a man and it finds that he is incapable of discharging his duty it lets him go but if it decides to.-keep him for a number of years in its employment it sees that he pays a certain *amount into the fund to provide for his retirement. That is a good system, but it is not the system we are adopting. We are appointing men and women for the public service at the rate of 660 a month many of whom are incapable, and we are now providing that the country shall take charge of them when they are retired.

maintopic: RETIREMENT OF MEMBERS OF PUBLIC SERVICE.

speechtext:
The
purpose of the Bill is one that I entirely sympathize with. It appears to be an effort on the part of the Government to care-or rather to give a measure of care-for inefficient and incapable public servants who may have been in the service for some time past and whom it now seeks to discharge. I think we perhaps may do these people who have been in the service of the country an injustice-I Tather think that in soime respects an injustice has been done to them today in the remarks that have been made by some hon. gentlemen. One of the evils of the patronage system in the past in Government appointments in this country has been to place in our Civil Service many inefficient, people, and that has happened far the last forty ye irs. Consequently we have in the Government service to this day men and women who secured their positions as a re-

suit of political pull or influence perhaps 25 or 30, or even 35 years ago, and have remained in the service ever since. Now it is all right to say that they should be turned adrift without anything in the way of pension or assistance at the time they sever their connection with the public service, but II think there is an obligation resting upon the country and upon the Government to give a measure of care to them. If I have any -criticism to offer it is along the line of that of my 'hon. friend from South Perth (Mr. Steele), that the Government might very well have been a little more generous in dealing with those classes that are referred to in these clauses. Now I take it, this legislation is not directed to the end of working out a permanent pension system. I believe in a permanent pension system, Mr. Speaker, in the public service, and I believe in it because it will pay the country to have it. I differ in that regard from my hon. friend from Elgin (Mr. Crothers). We find to-day that the most successful business corporations who employ large numbers of men are adopting a pension system. True, it may be in different forms, but nevertheless they are adopting the principle of the pension system. And why are they doing it? They frankly pult it on a basis of service-on the basis of dollars and cents if you like-for their business. There is nothing so harrassing to the person living on a small salary as the *f.ear of want in his old age, and I can conceive of this:	That a public employee
whose mind is troubled with such thoughts canndt bring an entirely clear head and clear judgment to bear on the duties he is discharging day by day. If you can assure him against the fear of want in old age, you are creating an atmosphere for him to work in, which wall result in his rendering more efficient service than he otherwise would; and consequently upon the basis of utility alone I think the principle of a pension in the public service-a principle which, as I say, large industrial corporations are adopting-can be defended and justified.

speechtext:
My hon. friend and I are travelling in the same diredtion to some extent:	The principle I think is a sound
principle; hut the matter should only be settled after full inquiry into ilt. It does appear to me that a principle that might well be adopted in the case of a permanent pension fund is (that whereby the employees and the Government both contribute to the creation of the fund. Certainly I am at one with my hon. friend from Elgin in the view that the employees should contribute to such a fund, and I think the Government might also very well add something to it. That pension should only come after a long period of service. We then could operate on this basis: That only efficient people should be taken into the public service and kept there. Then with such pension system, as the case may be where your public servant could look forward on retiring from the public service at the end of 25 or 30 or 35 years to something thalt will guard him against want in his old age, you have to my mind the conditions that will bring efficiency in the highest degree to your public service.
I have another criticism to make in respect to this matter and it is this: I am inclined to think, Mr. Speaker, that we are giving too much power to the Civil Service Commission in the matter of the administration of the public services. Now I am for a Civil Service Commission; I do not want to be misunderstood in that regard. I am free, however, to say this: That if I were again undertaking to administer a department of the Government I have sufficient conceit in myself to imagine that I could probably administer my department better without the aid of a Civil Service Commission. Still, I recognize that a department of the Government is different from an ordinary [DOT] business in many respects, and consequently that it is necessary and highly necessary, to have your Civil Service Commission. Nevertheless it is a mistake, in my judgment, to hamper the control of the staff of a department through the operation of the commission. After all, if you have men of sound judgment and ability at the head of your various branches of a department these men- who are in daily contact with the staff under them-in my judgment are best informed as to their efficiency and ability; and when you take the matter of controlling the staff largely out of their hands and give it into the control of the Civil Service Commission then you are creaking a condition of affairs that does not make for good discipline or efficiency in your departments. I recognize, Mr. Speaker, that on this point I may be trespassing some-

what beyond the bounds of this Bill, but the whole matter is relalted, and I am inclined to think that pe'rhaps we have erred a lifttle in charging the Civil Service Commission with too much responsibility in the control of the staff of our various departments.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Just a moment. At that time by reason of some irregularity in the proceedings by which these men were taken into the penitentiary they had not been legally brought in and therefore were not legally held under that commitment.
M r. BUREAU:	That is the gist of the
whole thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Will the hon. member
allow me to call his attention to something. It had not been held that the conviction was illegal, or that the sentence was illegal: they both stood as the judgment of a competent court ordering that one of these men should spend 25 years, and the other a lifetime in the penitentiary. Both conviction and sentence stood intact. With the execution of that judgment this department was not charged. The Attorney General of the province was charged with the duty of seeing that judgment-which stood absolutely intact-should be executed. One attempt to execute it had failed by reason of an irregularity, but the judgment was not satisfied: These men were men at liberty under sentence to be in the penitentiary.
Could they not have claimed "autrefois convict"?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
What I am trying to
point out is that Mr. Justice Duclos did not pretend to decide that they were not properly convicted. As I say, the judgment of the court stood. Now the law officers of the province of Quebec, at whose, head I am sure the hon. member will agree, is a very distinguished lawyer in the person of the Hon. Mr. Taschereau-and the head of the Government-a gentleman who was for years the Attorney General of the province of Quebec, and who I am sure nobody, certainly least of all my hon. friend (Mr. Le-rnieux), would question, is a lawyer of outstanding reputation-that Government and the Attorney General are by the law charged with the administration of justice and the enforcement of the judgments of the criminal court. They thought that it was their duty not to allow these men-men still under sentence

to go scot free because there had been some irregularity in the first steps taken to execute that judgment. As I say, there was an irregularity in the method of execution but the judgment stood. They may have been right or they may have been wrong, but they had a duty to discharge and that duty was to see to the enforcement of that judgment in accordance with the law. They were advised that since there was an irregularity in one commitment, and the judgment still stood, the proper thing to do was to issue a regular commitmentt. They therefore caused a commitment to be issued and a warrant to be delivered to Ithe proper officer of the court, and, as I said the other day, although that was no part of our obligation, we did feel that we should -allow our officers Ito be of assistance to these law authorities in so far as they might properly be so in connection with the execution of that warrant.
On that new commitment, these two men were brought to the penitentiary. The warden of the penitentiary had the previous week got an order from one	judge	to	release these men.
The following week arrives the pro-

per law officer with the new commitment emanating from the court ordering the warden to take these men in execution of the sentence, and he obeyed that order. I think the hon. gentleman will himself admit that the warden had no option to do otherwise.

Will not my hon. friend at once admit that Ithe expression "parody" is not too strong when we find that situation existing:	An officer haying to say
"Yes" to-day and "No" Ito-morrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not want to use
the expression, if my friend will pardon me, for the reason, that the "parody" is in the contradictory orders of the courts; and that is one of the very substantial reasons pointed out by the Supreme Court of Canada why a judge on habeas corpus should not, once lit appears to him that men are in jail under the judgment of a competent criminal coiuirlt, undertake Ibo let them oiut. It is not for him to decide Ithe regularity of the procedure of the Court of King's Bench. My hon. friend says that when a court makes a mistake there is a remedy by appeal. That is absolutely true. If Ithere was an irregularity in the proceedings of the Court of King's Bench under which these men were committed to the penitentiary, there was a remedy by writ of error -ot other proper recourse by way of appeal. I am not quite sure Ithat my hon. friend and I are not at the moment both guilty of contempt of court, because we are discussing questions which aire now actually pending before the Superior Court in Montreal.
The difficulty has arisen in this case that somebody has, with all respect, introduced into it, with the desire to create a sensation.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Then if it was not with that motive I am at a loss to know what motive prompted him. But let the motive go. Somebody has erroneously introduced into this matter the suggestion-which, of course, in its nature is sensational, whether it was his motive or not.-that there has been something in the nature of a rebellion on the part of the Attorney General of the province or of the Minister of Justice of Canada, In that regard I think the Minister of Justice has got an undue share of attention, if I may mention it, because I may say that so far I have not seen any criticism of the Attorney General of the province in regard to the procedure-and I am gUtad of tjhiat because he deserves no criticism, but however that may be, unfortunately there has crept into this matter

some comoeipltio'ni of the existence oif a desire to rebel against the orders of the court.
The order of Mr. Justice Ducloe having been obeyed, it was exhausted. As I say, at the instance of the law officers of the province a new .commitment was issued, and the officer of the court arrived at the penitentiary with the order of the Court of King's Bench that one of these men should be detained in the penitentiary for 25 years, and the other one for his life. Under the order the warden took charge of the two men. Then what happened? Counsel for these men made application for a new writ of habeas corpus. Now, I really think it is an unfortunate thing that I should be put in the position of having to discuss this matter at the present time, because whatever reputation may be sought to be given to me in this connection for lack of respect for the courts, I have the highest respect for the courts and this matter is actually before them. A second writ of habeas corpus :wias issued on a Saturady-I do not know at what hour. It was made returnable at half-past fen on Monday morning. It was served on Saturday night-I do not know at what hour. No notice was given to the Attorney General of the province, although according to a practice that always existed in the days when I practised law, and which I am assured on the highest authority still prevails in cases of that nature, it is the rule that notice should be given to the Attorney General of the province. No notice was given -to him. Sunday only was allowed to intervene between the service of the writ and its return. The order was to produce these men before a judge who was not the judge sitting in the practice court, but the judge who had issued the previous writ of habeas corpus. I am not suggesting that that affects his jurisdiction. I am only pointing out the chain of events. 'The order was made returnable in Room No. 4 of the court house -not in Room 31, which is where the practice court habitually sits and lawyers expect to go for practice matters. This Room No. 4, as no doubt hon. gentlemen familiar with the location know, is in a wing or annex of the courthouse.
At half-past ten on Monday morning the warden, in company with the representative of the Attorney General of the province, was in the practice court-the place, as I say, where such matters usually are dealt with. He was- there with his return, and that return, as I had occasion to mention the other day, was in the words of a return

which, under like circumstances, had been declared by the Supreme Court of Canada to be sufficient. Now, unfortunately, as I say, the writ was made returnable in another room, and the judge was in that other room, and there seems to have been some misunderstanding about it; but in any event, the judge, by reason of the non-production in that room of the two prisoners and the non-appearance of the warden, made an entry on the back of the writ ordering the liberation of the prisoners, and then proceeded to issue what is called "a rule nisi," which, as hon. gentlemen familiar with the form know, orders that in view of certain things a man shall be imprisoned, and in this instance he was* to be imprisoned for a year. But there is always the little saving clause at the end, "nisi causa contra." This rule, like all these rules, said: "Unless cause to the contrary be shown, on Monday next, the 21st of June."
Mr. LEM1EUX:	My facts are pretty accurate, then.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
said that the court decided that he had been guilty of contempt and ordered him to go to jail for a year. But if somebody made an application for contempt against any one of us, the rule that would issue would order that this man, having been guilty of contempt, be imprisoned for such a period of time unless cause to the contrary be shown. That is the rule which, I am informed, issued against Mr. Malepart. Mr. Malepart is represented by counsel and through his counsel will show cause on Monday morning, and then we will know whether or not Mr. Malepart was guilty of contempt. I do not want to discuss at all the effect of the writing on the back of the writ an order for the release of the men concerned. It would seem to me clear, whatever my opinion may be worth, that such an order would be at least premature. I think that anybody who gives the matter a moment's thought will realize that on a writ ordering the production of men for the purpose of ascertaining on what grounds they are held it is hardly possible for a judge, without any returns, to know the grounds on which they are held and to order their release. Hon. gentlemen will admit that for all that there was before that judge at the time in the form of a report, those men might have been convicted of an entirely different offence and committed again on an entirely different commitment. I do not think that that was intended to operate as an order for the release. However, I realize that there is a certain impropriety in my expressing these
opinions, because this matter is before the courts. When I had occasion to make a statement the other day I gave assurance that we would do our very best to have the *matter judicially disposed of. That is the extent of our disposition to be guilty of contempt of court. I omitted to say that the warden's return was filed; it is of record in the court. It was filed, if my information is correct, at 10.45, he having been in company with the representative of the Attorney General in the practice court in the court house in the city of Montreal for the purpose of having that return produced in the meantime. Now, so far as the suggestion of disobedience is concerned, out of this unfortunate
5 p.m. confusion about rooms has grown this mythical refusal, not only of the warden, but, I understand, of the Minister of Justice and of the Attorney General of the province, to obey a writ. Now, I do not want any confusion. It is the fact that the men were not actually produced that morning. And why? Because the warden was advised that there was not jurisdiction and that he should take the proper course that everybody takes when he thinks an order has been issued without jurisdiction: that is, that he should go before the court and most respectfully submit the reasons why he believes that the court has not jurisdiction, and that is what he did. I have not any doubt-well, I do not want to say that I have not aqy doubt about legal questions; I suppose that is not becoming, but my impression is that if we had not had this little mistake as .to rooms and that return had been put in before the judge the court then or later, if it thought it necessary to have the matter under advisement, would have decided the question that was then raised. As I understand it, that is among the questions which will come before the court on Monday morning. I may say that my information is that on Monday morning the matter will come before the Chief Justice of the province of Quebec .1 think hon. gentlemen will agree with me that it is a fortunate thing-
Chief Justice Archibald?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
What more jurisdiction has he?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
He has no more, but I was going to say that the judge who issued the first order and all of us are to be congratulated that there should be an opportunity of having the question, upon which there is difference of opinion, adjudicated

upon by a judge who has not already pronounced himself upon that important question of jurisdiction. That is all I am going to say; I do not suggest that the Chief Justice has any more jurisdiction than any other judge. The question of jurisdiction does not arise because the judge is a judge of the Superior Court rather than a judge of some other court. The question of jurisdiction that arises is this: The Habeas Corpus Act is in express terms made inapplicable to people who are held under the sentence or judgment of a competent criminal court-and, indeed, to people who are held under the judgment of .a civil court. The purpose of the writ of habeas corpus is to make sure that no man is detained without authority of law.
Without cause.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Without authority of law; that is the one satisfactory cause for detaining a man. I do not know what Mr. Justice Archibald will decide, and I am not here to criticise the decision of Mr. Justice Duclos. But my own opinion, based upon the advice of men in whose competency I have the very highest confidence, is that Mr. Justice Duclos had no jurisdiction. However, his writ was obeyed.
The second writ.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The writ that he maintained was obeyed. His second writ was obeyed to this extent: As I said I do not want to make confusion. I am not saying that the men were brought, but the warden made his return respectfully submitting to the court that because this man was held upon the sentence of	a competent
criminal court, he, the	warden, felt
it his duty to decline the jurisdiction. I want to say, just as bearing upon the possibility of there being any contempt in that, that if he was mistaken in doing that, he had behind him the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada that if his facts were aright that was the proper return to make. After all, it would be an extreme interpretation of the doctrine of contempt to say that a man following the decision of the Supreme 'Court of Canada as to what he ought to do was guilty of contempt. However, that is for the courts to decide. That matter will be tried out before a proper tribunal. I would not be going into this at all, if it were not that I do think that the mis-apprehension that appears to exist not only as to people's intentions but as to what was done, is most prejudicial to the administration of justice in this country. I

would like to add that in the judgment of the 'Supreme Court which I have just mentioned that is one of the results that is pointed out as being conclusive reasons why upon writ of habeas corpus, once it comes to the knowledge of the judge before whom the application for the writ is made that the man is there under judgment of a competent tribunal, he should stop. I am not going to introduce into the matter any question about the procedure of inferior tribunals. I express no opinion one way or the other upon that for the moment, because here we are not concerned with that. We are here concerned with the judgment of a Superior Court, the court especially charged with the administration of criminal justice in the province, and, as I say, in the judgment of the Supreme Court which I have mentioned, and of which I read an extract, this very creation of this regrettable situation is pointed out as one of the conclusive reasons in support of what is held to be the undoubted law, that under those circumstances when the judge -has before him sufficient to show the man is in the penitentiary or in jail upon the judgment of a court of competent jurisdiction it is time for him to say "My hands are off. This is not a case where I can undertake to decide w-hether he ought to be there or not." I say that with all respect to Mr. Justice Duclos, the position the warden was in, was that he found himself in face of the orders of two courts, one telling him to do one thing, and another telling him to do another. He comes to the court that made the last of these orders and says "I submit that under the circumstances you have no jurisdiction, and I do that very respectfully." That will be argued and decided.
I recognize the importance of the liberty of the subject, but if hon. gentlemen give one moment's thought to what would be our position, to what is our position in this country, if every individual judge in the country has authority when he thinks there is an irregularity in the proceedings of another court to release from our penitentiaries and jails any man confined therein no matter how clear it is that he was sentenced to be there, they will see it would be impossible to properly enforce the law in Ithis country. I say that with no disrespect. I am not suggesting that any judge would intentionally let a man out perversely, but if our system of law is such that the proceedings of all our criminal courts are subject to be set aside if there be found in the province or in the district any judge of a -Superior Court who is of the opinion that

the proceeding taken to convey to the warden of the penitentiary the information that the man was convicted was not sufficient how will it be possible to enforce law into this country?
I do not know that I have deallt at greater length with this matter than could be avoided once the question, is raised. I have made this explanation because, the question being raised, I felt that I owed it to my own consideration and. respect for the authority of the courts and the administration of justice to make it as clear as I could that this matter does not involve, as I see it, any contempt of Ithe court. Most assuredly it involves no intentional contempt of the court. It may be-it is not for me to decide-Ithat the submission to the court of a question whether it had jurisdiction was contempt; it is not for me to decide.
I only want Ito add this:	I have tried
1fco explain the facts. I do not want to argue. Perhaps it is that what was done was wrong; if so, the courts will so decide. I think that what was done was right; if so, the courts will so decide. I do ask that hon. gentlemen exclude from their minds this conception that what was done involves a disregard of law and an indisposition to bow to the orders of the court. 'There is the fact, and this ought nolt to be lost sight of, that the Attorney General of the province has duties as well as rights. He has a responsibility for the performance of those duties, and if he be of opinion that this sentence has not been satisfied and that it is his duty, as charged with the administration of justice and the enforcement of the law, to see that that sentence is satisfied, whether he be right in his opinion or not, surely if he be of that opinion he was but doing his duty in taking the legal process to bring about the execution of that sentence. He had been told that one commitment had been issued which did not contain all the things that in the opinion of Mr. Justice Duclos ought to be in it, and therefore the court held that that way of bringing him in was irregular. And (that he could not be held under that bringing of him in. Thereupon, if the Attorney General was convinced that it was his duty to see to the enforcement of that judgment, which sltill stood, and I would have shared that opinion, what course was open to him except to issue a new commitment, meet the objections that were made Ito the order that was issued by the court, and see that it was executed. Then, as has happened, there would be opportunities for the courts 244
to decide whether he was right or wrong in doing what he did. What was his alternative? His alternative was to sit quietly back wilthout exhausting the methods he 'believed to be open to him and say: "I am not concerned, I am willing to recognize that an avowed-murderer-I do not know that these men are avowed murderers, but if it applies in this case ilt will apply in any case-the circumstances of the conviction have nothing to do with it." The alternative he had was to say: "lit is a matter of pure indifference to me. I am willing to sit back and accept the situation that if a clerk leaves a line out in a commitment and the person committed is fortunate enough to gelt into the penitentiary under that commitment, with that line left out, the sentence of the court is gone forever. All his punishment is fulfilled, because somebody left out a line or two of the instrument, not the judgment, ordering Ithe transportation to the penitentiary." That is the quesltion to be decided, and the courts will decide it.
The impression has been created that the courts of our province are being overridden by certain authorities-I do not know who they are-and that judgments are not being respected.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have given you the
facts. Surely I cannot deal with impressions if I do not know what the fact is upon which they are based. I take it that they are based upon misinformation.

Let me give you a
straight statement of fact. These men were convicted and sentenced to the penitentiary. After they were in the penitentiary there was a writ of habeas corpus issued and they were released owing to irregularities. 'No judge interfered; nothing was. done. They were taken afterwards, without any order of the court, the habeas corpus still being in force-that is, so far as the facts are known to the public, and no doubt it was in force,-and are thrown bodily back into the penitentiary. By virtue of what authority was that done?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have told you, by virtue of the authority of the Court of King's Bench. Let me give the hon. gentleman what is a perfectly analagous case with which we are all absolutely familiar. A judgment in a civil case is rendered. II take my execution and issue a writ of seizure. I go and seize the defendant's goods, an irregularity creeps in, and opposition is made. That opposition is maintained; it is



decided that the way I tried to execute my judgment was irregular, and it is quashed. Then what do I do? My judgment is still there.

The opposition is fought in the courts.
Mr. (DOHERTY: Yes; and I take it that the first writ of habeas corpus was the opposition to the way of execution in this matter. It was decided that the way of execution was faulty.

It was not decided in
this case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
(On the first writ
of habeas carpus it was decided that the method of procedure of the officers of the court was irregular, and their proceeding was quashed just as my seizure was quashed in the hypothetical case I have given. So far, we agree, there is analogy. Now, with my seizure quashed I go back to the court but the court does not intervene at all by any action of the judge. I apply for a new writ of execution.
Certainly, a'new writ.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes; precisely what
was done in this case, but this is what the hon. gentleman apparently will not stop to apprehend. A new commitment was issued.
The court was no longer sitting.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It' does not need the court to draw up a commitment. [DOT] The commitment is the writ of execution which the officers of the court issue, and just as in my civil case, when I go for my second writ of execution I would not go to the judge but to the officer of the court, and say:	"There is my unsatisfied judgment;
will you give me another writ of execution, because last week or last month you gave me an irregular writ?"-so in this case it is the officer of the court on whom the responsibility rests.

The analogy does not
hold good in the case of a criminal action.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman so affirms, and that is what the court will decide.

Well, it seems to me, and it is apparently the old British tradition too, that in criminal matters you cannot decide anything without the presence of the prisoner, either personally or by his representative. Now, these prisoners were

absolutely free. They were released by writ of habeas corpus. Then the Attorney General or some one else, I do not know who, goes before the court, interviews the clerk, and gets another commitment. Where are the prisoners all that time? In the hands of your officers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
With all respect, I do
think that it is useless for me to try to bring conviction home to the hon. gentleman, because we understand this matter absolutely differently. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They were at liberty, with a judgment of the Court of King's Bench saying: "You ought to' be in penitentiary; I condemn you to spend twenty-five years in penitentiary." If he (was mas-taken there can be no. responsibility on me; so (why do. hon. gentlemen bring this matter before this House and suggest that in some way blame i!s to be attached to the Department of Justice?

speechtext: The officer of the court.
Of the Department of Justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The officer o!f the department was used for the purpose of identifying the prisoner. I do not want to be misunderstood [when I say that the responsibility for that proceeding is upon the Attorney General. That is undoubtedly true. It was for him to take the responsibility and he took it; and so far as responsibility may attach to me because I think he was right, I am perfectly frank to say that I do think he [was right. Of course, when I say "I," hoar, gentlemen will understand that it was not I .personally who was supervising the .proceeding, although I aim prepared to take the responsibility for what the officers of the department did. And 'they, .being convinced .that the Attorney . General was acting legally and properly- .and as a matter of fact, I doubt whether they rwould have been entitled to' act otherwise than, they did, .because it was for the Attorney General to assume the responsi-

bi'lity-they did provide an officer to go down and identify the prisoner. The responsibility fox that phase of the proceedings is clearly -with the Attorney General. But in saying that I wish it to be understood 'that I shark nothing. I never have shirked any responsibility in any event. I may have been wrong; I may ibe wrong this time; but the responsibility in this case is not with me. As custodians of the penitentiary the department in this matter is in a purely receptive position. 'If there is any blame it is on the Minister of Justice, and I will tell him why.

speechtext: Not for fifteen years, I think.

Not for fifteen years? Well, when the salaries of the judges have not been increased for the last fifteen years the

We all know-it has been said a hundred times in this House-that it costs at least a hundred per cent more to live to-day than it did fifteen years ago. I would like to add my

I understand that these salaries have been the same for fifteen years. Well, they were too low to start with, and they are very much more inadequate now owing to the increase in the cost of living that we hear so much about. This country has grown in importance very materially in the last fifteen years. Therefore the remuneration paid to the Chief Justice and the other judges of the Supreme Court- which a great many people would like to see made a court of last resort in this country-is simply absurd. The salaries which they receive are not at all in accordance with the dignity of their positions and, I understand, are totally inadequate, because we must remember that the gentlemen who occupy those distinguished positions must live in a manner befitting their rank. I perhaps could live on half the amount that they receive because I do not have to maintain anything like the same status that a judge in the Supreme Court is obliged to maintain. We must also remember that if the present judges were to vacate their positions, owing to death or other reasons it is doubtful whether qualified1 men could be got to fill the positions at the salaries now paid. I do not know that I am an advocate of the views of those who want to make the Supreme Court a court of last resort in Canada, because as long as we .are connected with Great Britain I think we

should avail ourselves of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. If, however, the Supreme Court of Canada erver comes to he the court of last resort better salaries will have to (be paid in order to attract men of the very highest type to that court. I urge, and urge very strongly, that the salaries of the Supreme Court judges be raised immediately to a reasonable basis, and that these judges be allowed a salary sufficient to enable them to live in accordance with the dignity of their position and of the importance of the country which they represent. Until recently the judges of the Supreme Court of the United 'States were practically in the same position as our own -if not even worse-with respect to the stipends they enjoyed; but I believe there has been an improvement in that respect owing no doubt to the fact that the Supreme Court of the adjoining Republic has come to be regarded as one of the great courts of the world1. In Canada, as we increase in population and in importance, we should recognize the fact that the -Supreme Court is virtually the court of final appeal so far as we are concerned, and should raise the salaries of -the judges to a figure -more in accordance with their high dignity and status. speechtext: This is simply a matter of reducing the capital stock of the company. They had to pay holders of capital stock par value-they have to get the consent of two-thirds of the stockholders, and also the consent of the Minister of Finance, before they can do anything.
